title: Harden the capstone and rehearse recovery
outcome: Release with verified permission, data, and recovery behaviour.
story: Before staff rely on the capstone, Amina asks what happens if a deployment fails or a customer tries to access another shop. Prove those answers with tests and a recovery rehearsal.

frames.explanation: A migration must preserve the existing information and obey its contract.
Silently changing bad data can make recovery harder.

sections.title: Review threats at each boundary
paragraphs: List assets, callers, trust boundaries, and likely failures. Test unauthorized reads/writes, changed approval, replay, unsafe HTML rendering, malformed model output, document injection, and private logging. Include provider egress and spending limits.

The lab is a pure-data migration exercise. It does not certify security. The real project requires direct requests that attempt the denied operations and inspection of actual database and log outcomes.

sections.title: Plan a migration before executing it
paragraphs: Describe the old schema, new schema, preserved fields, constraints, and invalid-data policy. Run a dry run on a copy. Verify row counts, ids, relationships, and representative records afterward.
Keep a verified backup and test restore. A rollback may require both application version and data restore. Never assume reversing a code commit reverses a database migration or an external operation.

sections.title: Harden the deployment
paragraphs: Serve over HTTPS with production cookie settings. Restrict accepted hosts and origins, set resource and request limits, and keep keys in server configuration. Pin dependencies and inspect the frontend bundle for accidental private configuration.

Use health and smoke checks from the release lesson. Configure log access and retention. Record who can deploy, approve risky actions, rotate keys, and recover data. The local learning accounts and localhost settings are not production credentials.

sections.title: Rehearse and retain evidence
paragraphs: Deploy a known version into a rehearsal environment with safe data. Attempt the cross-shop tests and a deliberate failed change. Restore the verified version and data, then repeat the main flow.

Publish a concise release record with commit, configuration mode, migration result, evaluation version, known limits, and recovery evidence. If a required check fails, fix it or keep the release blocked with a clear owner.

words.meaning: An account of what needs protection, from whom, and at which boundaries.
A controlled change to the structure or meaning of stored data.
Testing that a backup can recover the intended usable data.

example.code:
function migrate(rows){const ids=new Set();return rows.map(row=>{if(!Number.isInteger(row.id)||row.id<=0||ids.has(row.id))throw new RangeError("Invalid or duplicate id");ids.add(row.id);const status=row.status??"open";if(!["open","closed"].includes(status))throw new RangeError("Invalid status");return {...row,status};});}
console.log(migrate([{id:1,text:"Hello"}]));
explanation: A new object preserves the old fields.
The missing status gets the agreed default.
Invalid status or identifiers stop rather than silently repair records.

exercise.title: A non-mutating status migration
exercise.brief: Write migrate(rows). Preserve fields, add open for a missing/null status, keep open or closed, reject other statuses and invalid/duplicate positive integer ids with RangeError. The checker also verifies the supplied rows were not changed.

steps.title: Add a field without changing the source
steps.task: Return new row objects with the original fields and status defaulting to open.
steps.hint: Use map and object spread; do not assign row.status.

steps.title: Reject unknown statuses
steps.task: Only open and closed are accepted after applying the default.
steps.hint: Validate before returning the new row.
steps.solution: function migrate(rows){return rows.map(row=>{const status=row.status??"open";if(!["open","closed"].includes(status))throw new RangeError("Invalid status");return {...row,status};});}

steps.title: Validate record identity
steps.task: Require unique positive integer ids. Preserve the original input even when successful.
steps.hint: Track seen ids in a Set.
steps.solution: function migrate(rows){const ids=new Set();return rows.map(row=>{if(!Number.isInteger(row.id)||row.id<=0||ids.has(row.id))throw new RangeError("Invalid or duplicate id");ids.add(row.id);const status=row.status??"open";if(!["open","closed"].includes(status))throw new RangeError("Invalid status");return {...row,status};});}

cases.label: An old row
cases.why: Preserve data and leave the input untouched.

cases.label: An existing closed row
cases.why: Do not reset a valid existing status.

cases.label: No stored rows
cases.why: An empty migration has a defined outcome.

project.title: A hardened release and rollback
project.brief: Perform a threat review, data migration rehearsal, and rollback of the real capstone with safe data. Preserve the evidence for a reviewer.
deliverables: A boundary-specific threat and test matrix.
A versioned release and recovery runbook.

milestones.title: Test the boundaries
actions: Test approval change, expiry, and replay.
Inspect rendering, provider validation, and safe logs.

milestones.title: Rehearse data change
actions: Back up and verify the restored copy.
Migrate a copy and compare rows and relationships.
Record whether rollback requires data restore.

milestones.title: Release and recover
actions: Build a known commit with production configuration documented.
Run health and main-flow smoke checks.
Restore after a deliberate failure and repeat the checks.

acceptance: Denied operations cannot change protected data.
Secrets stay out of client code and logs.
Migration preserves intended records and constraints.
Rollback produces a usable main flow.

tests.expected: It stops with no silent data rewrite.

tests.situation: A release fails its smoke test
tests.expected: The verified earlier version and intended data are restored.

project.extension: Arrange an independent security review and address one reproduced finding with a focused regression test.
reflection: Which test checked the real boundary?
What would rolling back code fail to restore?
What evidence supports the release decision?
